sentences.zh: 皇甫謐

translations.literal: Huangfu Mi.
translations.idiomatic: Huangfu Mi

sentences.zh: 皇甫謐，字士安，幼名靜，安定朝那人，漢太尉嵩之曾孫也。

translations.literal: Huangfu Mi, courtesy name Shi’an, childhood name Jing, was a man of Chaona in Anding, a great-grandson of Han Grand Commandant Song.
translations.idiomatic: Huangfu Mi, style Shi’an, childhood name Jing, came from Chaona in Anding commandery. He was a great-grandson of the Han grand commandant Huangfu Song.

sentences.zh: 出叔父，徙居新安。

translations.literal: He went out to his uncle’s line and moved residence to Xin’an.
translations.idiomatic: He was given in adoption to an uncle and moved with that branch to Xin’an.

sentences.zh: 年二十，不好學，遊蕩無度，或以為癡。

translations.literal: At age twenty he did not love learning, roamed and wandered without measure; some thought him stupid.
translations.idiomatic: At twenty he still shunned study, idled without restraint, and people took him for a simpleton.

sentences.zh: 嘗得瓜果，輒進所叔母任氏。

translations.literal: When he obtained melons and fruits, he always presented them to his uncle’s wife, Lady Ren.
translations.idiomatic: Whenever he had fruit, he brought it first to his aunt by adoption, Lady Ren.

sentences.zh: 任氏曰：「《孝經》云：『三牲之養，猶為不孝。

translations.literal: Lady Ren said, “The Classic of Filial Piety says, ‘With the three sacrificial beasts’ nurture, still there is unfilial conduct.’
translations.idiomatic: Lady Ren said, “The *Classic of Filial Piety* warns that even offering parents the three sacrificial meats can still be unfilial.”

sentences.zh: 』汝今年餘二十，目不存教，心不入道，無以慰我。

translations.literal: ’You this year exceed twenty; your eyes do not keep teaching; your heart does not enter the Way; there is nothing by which to console me.”
translations.idiomatic: You are past twenty yet pay no mind to instruction and give no thought to the Way—you cannot comfort me so.”

sentences.zh: 」因歎曰：「昔孟母三徙以成仁，曾父烹豕以存教，豈我居不卜鄰，教有所闕，何爾魯鈍之甚也！

translations.literal: ” Thereupon she sighed, saying, “Formerly Mencius’ mother thrice moved to complete benevolence; Zeng’s father cooked a pig to preserve teaching—was it that I did not choose neighbors by divination, that teaching had some lack—why are you so dull and blunt!”
translations.idiomatic: She sighed, “Mencius’ mother moved three times to find a good neighborhood; Zengzi’s father kept a promise to butcher a pig for the boy’s lesson. Have I failed to choose neighbors wisely, or left some gap in your upbringing, that you remain so thick-witted?”

sentences.zh: 修身篤學，自汝得之，于我何有！

translations.literal: Cultivating the body and earnest study—by yourself you obtain them; what is it to me!”
translations.idiomatic: Moral self-culture and real learning are yours to win or lose—they are not mine to give!”

sentences.zh: 」因對之流涕。

translations.literal: ” Thereupon facing him she wept tears.
translations.idiomatic: With that she wept before him.

sentences.zh: 謐乃感激，就鄉人席坦受書，勤力不怠。

translations.literal: Mi was then moved; he went to fellow townsman Xi Tan to receive books, and was diligent without slackening.
translations.idiomatic: Stricken with remorse, he went to the local scholar Xi Tan to study and worked without slackening.

sentences.zh: 居貧，躬自稼穡，帶經而農，遂博綜典籍百家之言。

translations.literal: Dwelling in poverty, he personally plowed and reaped, girded the classics while farming; thereupon he broadly combined canonical texts and the hundred schools’ words.
translations.idiomatic: Poor, he worked his own fields with a copy of the classics tucked in his belt until he had mastered the canon and the philosophers.

sentences.zh: 沈靜寡欲，始有高尚之志，以著述為務，自號玄晏先生。

translations.literal: Deep, quiet, with few desires, he first had lofty aims, took writing as his task, styled himself Master Xuanyan.
translations.idiomatic: Calm and detached, he resolved on a scholar’s life, devoted himself to authorship, and took the sobriquet Master Xuanyan.

sentences.zh: 著《禮樂》、《聖真》之論。

translations.literal: He composed treatises on ‘Ritual and Music’ and ‘Sagely Truth.’
translations.idiomatic: He wrote essays titled *Ritual and Music* and *Sagely Truth*.

sentences.zh: 後得風痹疾，猶手不輟卷。

translations.literal: Later he contracted wind-numbness illness, yet still his hand did not stop rolls.
translations.idiomatic: Later he fell ill with wind paralysis, yet never set his scrolls aside.

sentences.zh: 或勸謐修名廣交，謐以為「非聖人孰能兼存出處，居田里之中亦可以樂堯、舜之道，何必崇接世利，事官鞅掌，然後為名乎」。

translations.literal: Some urged Mi to cultivate fame and widen associations; Mi held that "unless one is a sage, who can keep both withdrawal and emergence? Dwelling in field and hamlet, one may still take joy in the way of Yao and Shun—why must one exalt joining worldly profit, serve in office busily busy, and only then be famed?"
translations.idiomatic: When urged to network for reputation, he replied that only a sage could combine reclusion and office; a man could find Yao and Shun’s Way in a village lane without chasing power and juggling posts.

sentences.zh: 作《玄守論》以答之，曰：

translations.literal: He composed the "Treatise on Mysterious Guarding" to answer them, saying:
translations.idiomatic: He answered in his *Treatise on Mysterious Guarding*:

sentences.zh: 遂不仕。

translations.literal: Thereupon he did not serve in office.
translations.idiomatic: He never took office.

sentences.zh: 耽玩典籍，忘寢與食，時人謂之「書淫」。

translations.literal: He indulged in and played with canonical texts, forgetting sleep and food; people of the time called him "book debauchee."
translations.idiomatic: He lost himself in books, forgetting meals and sleep, until contemporaries called him a "book drunkard."

sentences.zh: 或有箴其過篤，將損耗精神。

translations.literal: Some admonished him that his excess was too deep and would waste spirit.
translations.idiomatic: Friends warned that his fanaticism would ruin his health.

sentences.zh: 謐曰：「朝聞道，夕死可矣，況命之修短分定懸天乎！」

translations.literal: Mi said, "In the morning I hear the Way; in the evening I may die—how much more are life’s length and shortness allotted and hung on Heaven!"
translations.idiomatic: He answered, "The Analects say that hearing the Way at dawn leaves one content to die at dusk—what room is there to fret over fate?"

sentences.zh: 叔父有子既冠，謐年四十喪所生後母，遂還本宗。

translations.literal: His uncle had a son already capped; Mi at forty mourned the birth mother who had raised him, then returned to his original clan.
translations.idiomatic: When his uncle’s son came of age, Mi at forty buried the stepmother who had reared him and rejoined his birth father’s line.

sentences.zh: 城陽太守梁柳，謐從姑子也，當之官，人勸謐餞之。

translations.literal: Administrator of Chengyang Liang Liu was Mi’s aunt’s son; when about to take office, people urged Mi to give him a farewell feast.
translations.idiomatic: Liang Liu of Chengyang, his cousin on the distaff side, was leaving for a post; friends pressed Mi to host a parting banquet.

sentences.zh: 謐曰：「柳為布衣時過吾，吾送迎不出門，食不過鹽菜，貧者不以酒肉為禮。

translations.literal: Mi said, "When Liu was in plain cloth he visited me; I did not go beyond the gate to see him off or in, and food did not pass salted vegetables—the poor do not use wine and meat as ritual.
translations.idiomatic: Mi said, "When Liang Liu was still a commoner I never stepped past my gate to escort him, and we dined on pickled greens alone—the poor do not toast with meat and wine."

sentences.zh: 今作郡而送之，是貴城陽太守而賤梁柳，豈中古人之道，是非吾心所安也。」

translations.literal: Now that he becomes commandery governor and I send him off, this is to honor the Administrator of Chengyang and slight Liang Liu—how can that hit the way of the ancients? It is not what my heart can rest in."
translations.idiomatic: To fete him now that he wears a governor’s seal would honor the office and slight the man—hardly the ancient way, and not what my conscience allows."

sentences.zh: 時魏郡召上計掾，舉孝廉；

translations.literal: At that time Wei commandery summoned him as accounting clerk;
translations.idiomatic: Wei commandery summoned him as chief clerk for the capital report;

sentences.zh: 景元初，相國辟，皆不行。

translations.literal: at the start of the Jingyuan era, the minister of state summoned him; in all cases he did not go.
translations.idiomatic: Early in the Jingyuan era the minister of state summoned him again—he still refused.

sentences.zh: 其後鄉親勸令應命，謐為《釋勸論》以通志焉。

translations.literal: Afterward townsmen urged him to obey summons; Mi composed the "Treatise Releasing Persuasion" to express his intent.
translations.idiomatic: When neighbors pressed him to serve, he set out his resolve in *Releasing Persuasion*.

sentences.zh: 其辭曰：其後武帝頻下詔敦逼不已，謐上疏自稱草莽臣曰：「臣以尪弊，迷於道趣，因疾抽簪，散發林阜，人綱不閑，鳥獸為群。

translations.literal: Its wording said: Afterward Emperor Wu repeatedly issued edicts urging him without cease; Mi submitted a memorial styling himself "your grass-and-thicket subject," saying, "Your subject, being weak and ruined, lost himself in the Way’s pursuits; because of illness he plucked his hairpin and scattered hair in forest hill; human nets he does not practice; with birds and beasts he forms herds."
translations.idiomatic: The piece opens with a flourish, then turns to the emperor’s repeated summons: Mi styled himself a "weed-country subject," pleading that frailty had driven him to the hills among beasts, far from human ties.

sentences.zh: 陛下披榛采蘭，並收蒿艾。

translations.literal: "Your Majesty parts thorns to gather orchids, and together gathers mugwort."
translations.idiomatic: "Your Majesty," he wrote, "sifts the wilds for talent and gathers sage and commoner alike."

sentences.zh: 是以皋陶振褐，不仁者遠。

translations.literal: "Therefore Gao Yao shook his coarse cloak and the unkindly went far."
translations.idiomatic: "So Gao Yao once shook out his rustic cloak and the wicked fled."

sentences.zh: 臣惟頑蒙，備食晉粟，猶識唐人擊壤之樂，宜赴京城，稱壽闕外。

translations.literal: "Your subject alone is stubbornly dull, yet shares Jin’s grain; still he knows the Tang people’s joy of clapping earth—he ought to hasten to the capital and wish long life outside the palace."
translations.idiomatic: "Though a dullard fed at the Jin court, I still remember the simple joy of the ancients—I should rush to the capital to cheer your reign."

sentences.zh: 而小人無良，致災速禍，久嬰篤疾，軀半不仁，右腳偏小，十有九載。

translations.literal: "Yet the petty man lacks good conduct, bringing disaster and hastening misfortune; long he has been bound in grave illness, his body half without feeling, the right foot slightly small, for nine-tenths of nineteen years."
translations.idiomatic: "Yet vice has brought calamity: I have lain gravely ill for years, half my body numb, my right foot shrunken, for the better part of two decades."

sentences.zh: 又服寒食藥，違錯節度，辛苦荼毒，於今七年。

translations.literal: "Further he took cold-food powder, mistaking regulation; bitterly he suffered poison; up to now seven years."
translations.idiomatic: "Cold-food elixirs, wrongly dosed, have tormented me seven years."

sentences.zh: 隆冬裸袒食冰，當暑煩悶，加以咳逆，或若溫虐，或類傷寒，浮氣流腫，四肢酸重。

translations.literal: "In deep winter he went naked and ate ice; in summer heat vexed and stifled, added cough and reversal, sometimes like warm malaria, sometimes like cold damage; floating qi flowed swelling, four limbs sore and heavy."
translations.idiomatic: "In winter I shivered naked on ice; in summer I gasped with fever, cough, chills like malaria or typhoid, limbs swollen and leaden."

sentences.zh: 於今困劣，救命呼噏，父兄見出，妻息長訣。

translations.literal: "By now exhausted and weak, calling for rescue and breath, fathers and brothers see him out, wives and children long farewell."
translations.idiomatic: "Now I can only cry for breath while kin stand by for my last breath and my wife and children take their leave."

sentences.zh: 仰迫天威，扶輿就道，所苦加焉，不任進路，委身待罪，伏枕歎息。

translations.literal: "Pressed by Heaven’s awesomeness, leaning on a litter he took the road; his suffering increased; he could not bear advancing on the road; he entrusted his body awaiting guilt, lying on the pillow sighing."
translations.idiomatic: "Forced by imperial majesty onto a litter, I grow worse by the mile; I lay down my body and await judgment, sighing on my pillow."

sentences.zh: 臣聞《韶》《衛》不並奏，《雅》《鄭》不兼禦，故郤子入周，禍延王叔；

translations.literal: "Your subject has heard that Shao and Wei are not played together, Ya and Zheng are not both driven—therefore when Xi Ke entered Zhou, disaster extended to Prince Shu;
translations.idiomatic: "As fine music cannot mix with vulgar strains, so when a flawed man entered Zhou the king suffered—"

sentences.zh: 虞丘稱賢，樊姬掩口。

translations.literal: Yuqiu praised worthiness, Fan Ji covered her mouth.
translations.idiomatic: "Virtue and vice do not share one vessel, as when Fan Ji silenced her lord’s praise of a pretty face."

sentences.zh: 君子小人，禮不同器，況臣糠䵃，糅之彫胡？

translations.literal: "Gentleman and petty man, ritual does not share one vessel—how much more your subject, chaff and husks, blended with fine foxtail millet?"
translations.idiomatic: "Noble and base cannot share one bowl—how much less this chaff with your fine grain?"

sentences.zh: 庸夫錦衣，不稱其服也。

translations.literal: A common fellow in brocade robes does not match his garments.
translations.idiomatic: A peasant in silk never fits the cloth.

sentences.zh: 竊聞同命之士，咸以畢到，唯臣疾疢，抱釁床蓐，雖貪明時，懼斃命路隅。

translations.literal: "Your subject has heard that fellows of the same summons have all arrived; only your subject’s illness festers, embracing fault on bed-mat; though he covets the bright age, he fears collapsing dead beside the road."
translations.idiomatic: "Others summoned with me have reached the capital; I alone lie sick in bed, fearing I would die on the road if I tried."

sentences.zh: 設臣不疾，已遭堯、舜之世，執志箕山，猶當容之。

translations.literal: "Suppose your subject were not ill, already encountering Yao and Shun’s age, yet holding resolve at Mount Ji, still he ought to be accommodated."
translations.idiomatic: "Even in a Yao-Shun age a man set on Mount Ji’s reclusion would be indulged—how much more I?"

sentences.zh: 臣聞上有明聖之主，下有輸實之臣；

translations.literal: "Your subject has heard that above there is a bright sage lord; below there are ministers who convey substance;
translations.idiomatic: "Where the throne is wise, ministers speak plain truth;"

sentences.zh: 上有在寬之政，下有委情之人。

translations.literal: "above there is a policy of lenience; below there are men who entrust their feelings."
translations.idiomatic: "where policy is gentle, subjects may bare their hearts."

sentences.zh: 唯陛下留神垂恕，更旌瑰俊，索隱于傅岩，收釣於渭濱，無令泥滓久濁清流。

translations.literal: "Only may Your Majesty attend and show forgiveness, further mark rare talent, seek the hidden at Fu Yan, gather the angler on the Wei bank—do not let mud and mire long turbid the clear stream."
translations.idiomatic: "I beg you to forgive me, seek worthies at Fu Yan and the Wei River, and keep the muddy from fouling the clear current."

sentences.zh: 」謐辭切言至，遂見聽許。

translations.literal: "” Mi’s words were cutting and speech reached the mark; thereupon he was heard and permitted.
translations.idiomatic: The throne granted his plea when his memorial struck home.

sentences.zh: 歲餘，又舉賢良方正，並不起。

translations.literal: After more than a year, again he was recommended worthy and upright; in both cases he did not rise.
translations.idiomatic: A year later the court nominated him as worthy and upright; again he stayed home.

sentences.zh: 自表就帝借書，帝送一車書與之。

translations.literal: He personally memorialized to borrow books from the emperor; the emperor sent one cart of books to him.
translations.idiomatic: He asked the emperor for books and received a whole cartload from the palace.

sentences.zh: 謐雖羸疾，而披閱不怠。

translations.literal: Although Mi was emaciated by illness, yet he unrolled and read without slackening.
translations.idiomatic: Wasted by sickness, he never stopped reading.

sentences.zh: 初服寒食散，而性與之忤，每委頓不倫，嘗悲恚，叩刃欲自殺，叔母諫之而止。

translations.literal: At first he took cold-food dispersal, but his nature opposed it; each time he collapsed in disorder, once in grief and rage he knocked a blade wishing to kill himself; his aunt remonstrated and he stopped.
translations.idiomatic: Cold-food powders clashed with his constitution and left him in spasms; once, in despair, he drew a knife to end his life until his aunt stayed his hand.

sentences.zh: 濟陰太守蜀人文立，表以命士有贄為煩，請絕其禮幣，詔從之。

translations.literal: Administrator of Jiyin Wen Li of Shu memorialized that for summoned scholars the gift tribute was troublesome; he requested to cut off their ritual silk; an edict followed him.
translations.idiomatic: Wen Li, governor of Jiyin, asked to end the silk gifts required of summoned scholars, and the throne agreed.

sentences.zh: 謐聞而歎曰：「亡國之大夫不可與圖存，而以革歷代之制，其可乎！

translations.literal: Mi heard and sighed, saying, "A defeated state’s grandees may not plot survival—yet to alter dynastic precedent—can it be so!"
translations.idiomatic: Huangfu Mi groaned, "A minister of a fallen state should not redraw the rites of every age!"

sentences.zh: 夫『束帛戔戔』，《易》之明義，玄纁之贄，自古之舊也。

translations.literal: As for "bundled silk abundant," it is the Changes' clear meaning; dark-crimson tribute has been the custom since antiquity.
translations.idiomatic: "The *Book of Changes* sanctifies modest gifts of silk; dark and light silks have always opened the way to office."

sentences.zh: 故孔子稱夙夜強學以待問，席上之珍以待聘。

translations.literal: Therefore Confucius praised studying hard day and night to await questioning, treasures on the mat to await being hired.
translations.idiomatic: Confucius praised scholars who study nightly for the questions a lord will ask and keep their talents ready like treasures on the mat.

sentences.zh: 士於是乎三揖乃進，明致之難也；

translations.literal: Only then does the gentleman thrice bow and advance—clarifying that arriving is hard;
translations.idiomatic: Hence the triple bow before entering—accepting office is meant to be hard.

sentences.zh: 一讓而退，明去之易也。

translations.literal: once yielding he withdraws—clarifying that leaving is easy.
translations.idiomatic: One courteous refusal and he may withdraw—leaving should be easy.

sentences.zh: 若殷湯之于伊尹，文王之于太公，或身即莘野，或就載以歸，唯恐禮之不重，豈吝其煩費哉！

translations.literal: Such as Tang of Yin toward Yi Yin, King Wen toward the Grand Duke—sometimes the body went to Shen’s wilds, sometimes he was carried home in the cart—only fearing ritual was not heavy; how could they stint trouble and expense!
translations.idiomatic: Tang met Yi Yin in the fields; Wen carried Lü Shang home in his cart—they worried only that the rites were not lavish enough.

sentences.zh: 且一禮不備，貞女恥之，況命士乎！

translations.literal: Moreover if one rite is not complete, a chaste woman is shamed by it—how much more a summoned scholar!
translations.idiomatic: A chaste girl blushes if one rite is missing—how much more a gentleman summoned to court!

sentences.zh: 孔子曰：『賜也，爾愛其羊，我愛其禮。

translations.literal: Confucius said, "Ci, you spare the sheep; I spare the rite."
translations.idiomatic: Confucius told Zigong, "You would save the sheep; I would save the ritual."

sentences.zh: 』棄之如何？

translations.literal: 'To cast it away—how so?
translations.idiomatic: To abolish such gifts—what then?

sentences.zh: 政之失賢，於此乎在矣。」

translations.literal: Government’s losing worthies lies herein."
translations.idiomatic: That is how a state loses its best men."

sentences.zh: 咸甯初，又詔曰：「男子皇甫謐沈靜履素，守學好古，與流俗異趣，其以謐為太子中庶子。

translations.literal: At the start of the Xianning era, again an edict said, "The man Huangfu Mi is deep, quiet, treads plainness, guards learning and loves antiquity; with vulgar custom he shares a different bent; let Mi be made junior mentor to the heir."
translations.idiomatic: Early in Xianning the court named him junior mentor to the crown prince, praising his learning and distance from vulgar fashion.

sentences.zh: 」謐固辭篤疾。

translations.literal: "” Mi firmly declined grave illness.
translations.idiomatic: He pleaded grave illness and refused.

sentences.zh: 帝初雖不奪其志，尋復發詔徵為議郎，又召補著作郎。

translations.literal: The emperor at first although did not seize his intent, soon again issued edict summoning him as gentleman consultant, again summoned him to supplement compiler.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor yielded at first, then summoned him as gentleman consultant and later as palace compiler.

sentences.zh: 司隸校尉劉毅請為功曹，並不應。

translations.literal: Metropolitan commandant Liu Yi requested him as merit assessor; in both cases he did not respond.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Yi, metropolitan commandant, wanted him as merit clerk—again he stayed silent.

sentences.zh: 著論為葬送之制，名曰《篤終》，曰：而竟不仕。

translations.literal: He composed a treatise on burial rites, titled "Steadfast to the End," saying: yet in the end he never served.
translations.idiomatic: He wrote *Steadfast to the End* on simple burial, yet never took office.

sentences.zh: 卒，時年六十八。

translations.literal: He died at age sixty-eight.
translations.idiomatic: He died at sixty-eight.

sentences.zh: 子童靈、方回等遵其遺命。

translations.literal: Sons Tongling, Fanghui and others followed his dying commands.
translations.idiomatic: His sons Tongling and Fanghui carried out his last wishes.

sentences.zh: 謐所著詩賦誄頌論難甚多，又撰《帝王世紀》、《年曆》、《高士》、《逸士》、《列女》等傳、《玄晏春秋》，並重於世。

translations.literal: Mi’s composed odes, rhapsodies, dirges, hymns, treatises, and disputations were very many; he also compiled Records of Emperors and Ages, calendars, biographies of lofty and reclusive gentlemen, *Exemplary Women*, and *Xuanyan’s Spring and Autumn*—all were weighty in the generation.
translations.idiomatic: He left a large body of poetry and prose plus *Records of Emperors*, chronologies, accounts of recluses and heroines, and *Master Xuanyan’s Annals*, all esteemed in his time.

sentences.zh: 門人摯虞、張軌、牛綜、席純，皆為晉名臣。

translations.literal: Disciples Zhi Yu, Zhang Gui, Niu Zong, and Xi Chun all became famous Jin ministers.
translations.idiomatic: His pupils Zhi Yu, Zhang Gui, Niu Zong, and Xi Chun rose to high office under Jin.

translations.literal: Equals sign in the edition.
translations.idiomatic: The edition inserts a stray equals sign.

sentences.zh: 子方回

translations.literal: Son Fanghui.
translations.idiomatic: Son: Huangfu Fanghui

sentences.zh: =方回少遵父操，兼有文才。

translations.literal: Equals sign: Fanghui in youth followed his father’s conduct and also had literary talent.
translations.idiomatic: Huangfu Fanghui, in youth, followed his father’s way and showed literary gifts.

sentences.zh: 永嘉初，博士征，不起。

translations.literal: At the start of the Yongjia era, erudit summoned; he did not rise.
translations.idiomatic: When Yongjia opened he was summoned as erudit but would not go.

sentences.zh: 避亂荊州，閉戶閒居，未嘗入城府。

translations.literal: He avoided chaos in Jingzhou, closed door and dwelt idle, never entered the commandery seat.
translations.idiomatic: He fled the wars to Jingzhou, kept his door shut, and never entered the yamen.

sentences.zh: 蠶而後衣，耕而後食，先人後己，尊賢愛物，南土人士咸崇敬之。

translations.literal: After silkworms then he clothed; after plowing then he ate; others first, himself later; he honored worthies and cherished things; southern gentlemen all revered him.
translations.idiomatic: He clothed himself after the silkworms, ate after the harvest, put others first, honored the worthy, and won the south’s respect.

sentences.zh: 刺史陶侃禮之甚厚。

translations.literal: Inspector Tao Kan treated him very generously.
translations.idiomatic: Governor Tao Kan honored him lavishly.

sentences.zh: 侃每造之，著素士服，望門輒下而進。

translations.literal: Whenever Kan went to visit him, he wore plain scholar dress; seeing the gate he dismounted and entered.
translations.idiomatic: Tao Kan always donned plain robes and dismounted at his gate out of respect.

sentences.zh: 王敦遣從弟暠代侃，遷侃為廣州。

translations.literal: Wang Dun sent his cousin Hao to replace Kan and transferred Kan to Guangzhou.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Dun sent his cousin Wang Hao to replace Tao Kan and moved Kan to Guangzhou.

sentences.zh: 侃將詣敦，方回諫曰：「吾聞敵國滅，功臣亡。

translations.literal: As Kan was about to visit Dun, Fanghui remonstrated, saying, "I have heard that when an enemy state perishes, the merit minister perishes."
translations.idiomatic: When Tao Kan prepared to answer Wang Dun’s summons, Fanghui warned, "They say that once the foe is gone the strong general is next."

sentences.zh: 足下新破杜弢，功莫與二，欲無危，其可得乎！

translations.literal: "You have just crushed Du Tao; none can rival your merit—yet do you think you can stay out of danger?"
translations.idiomatic: "You have just crushed Du Tao and outshine every rival—do you imagine you can stay safe?"

sentences.zh: 」侃不從而行。

translations.literal: "” Kan did not follow but went.
translations.idiomatic: Tao Kan went anyway.

sentences.zh: 敦果欲殺侃，賴周訪獲免。

translations.literal: Dun indeed wished to kill Kan; relying on Zhou Fang he escaped.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Dun did try to kill him; Zhou Fang saved him.

sentences.zh: 暠既至荊州，大失物情，百姓叛暠迎杜弢。

translations.literal: When Hao reached Jingzhou, he greatly lost the people’s sentiment; commoners rebelled against Hao and welcomed Du Tao.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Hao so mishandled Jingzhou that the people rose for Du Tao against him.

sentences.zh: 暠大行誅戮以立威，以方回為侃所敬，責其不來詣己，乃收而斬之。

translations.literal: Hao greatly carried out executions and slaughter to establish awe; because Fanghui was one Kan respected, he blamed him for not coming to himself; thereupon he seized and beheaded him.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Hao butchered people to assert authority; because Fanghui was honored by Tao Kan, Hao executed him for refusing a personal call.

sentences.zh: 荊土華夷，莫不流涕。

translations.literal: Jingzhou’s Chinese and barbarians, none did not weep tears.
translations.idiomatic: Chinese and non-Chinese alike in Jingzhou wept for him.

sentences.zh: 摯虞

translations.literal: Zhi Yu.
translations.idiomatic: Zhi Yu

sentences.zh: 摯虞，字仲洽，京兆長安人也。

translations.literal: Zhi Yu, courtesy name Zhongqia, was a man of Chang’an in Jingzhao.
translations.idiomatic: Zhi Yu, style Zhongqia, came from Chang’an in Jingzhao commandery.

sentences.zh: 父模，魏太僕卿。

translations.literal: His father Mo was Wei Grand Coachman.
translations.idiomatic: His father Zhi Mo had been Wei’s Grand Coachman.

sentences.zh: 虞少事皇甫謐，才學通博，著述不倦。

translations.literal: Yu in youth served Huangfu Mi; his talent and learning were comprehensive and broad; he wrote tirelessly.
translations.idiomatic: He studied under Huangfu Mi, mastered wide learning, and wrote constantly.

sentences.zh: 郡檄主簿。

translations.literal: The commandery ordered him chief clerk.
translations.idiomatic: The commandery appointed him chief clerk.

sentences.zh: 虞嘗以死生有命，富貴在天。

translations.literal: Yu once held that death and life have fate, wealth and honor are with Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: He held that life and death are fated, wealth and rank lie with Heaven.

sentences.zh: 天之所祐者義也，人之所助者信也。

translations.literal: What Heaven blesses is righteousness; what men help is trustworthiness.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven favors the righteous; men aid the trustworthy.

sentences.zh: 履信思順，所以延福，違此而行，所以速禍。

translations.literal: Treading trustworthiness and thinking compliance thereby extends blessing; violating this and acting hastens misfortune.
translations.idiomatic: Faith and humility prolong good fortune; their opposite hastens disaster.

sentences.zh: 然道長世短，禍福舛錯，怵迫之徒，不知所守，蕩而積憤，或迷或放。

translations.literal: Yet the Way is long and generations short; misfortune and fortune cross; alarmed and pressed men do not know what to keep; they drift and pile resentment, sometimes lost, sometimes reckless.
translations.idiomatic: Yet life is short and the Way long; fortune twists; frightened men lose their bearings and swing between despair and recklessness.

sentences.zh: 故借之以身，假之以事，先陳處世不遇之難，遂棄彝倫，輕舉遠遊，以極常人罔惑之情，而後引之以正，反之以義，推神明之應於視聽之表，崇否泰之運于智力之外，以明天任命之不可違，故作《思遊賦》。

translations.literal: Therefore he lent it through the body, borrowed it through affairs, first setting forth the hardship of not meeting the age, then abandoning constant relations, lightly rising and roaming far, to exhaust ordinary men’s unguided feelings, afterward leading them with rectitude, returning them with duty, pushing spirit illumination’s response beyond seeing and hearing, elevating fortune’s turn beyond wit and strength, to clarify that Heaven’s command may not be disobeyed; therefore he made the "Rhapsody on Pondering Roaming."
translations.idiomatic: So in *Rhapsody on Pondering Roaming* he first paints worldly frustration and escapist fantasy, then turns the reader back to moral duty and Heaven’s decree.

sentences.zh: 其辭曰：舉賢良，與夏侯湛等十七人策為下第，拜中郎。

translations.literal: Its wording said: He was recommended worthy and good; with Xiahou Zhan and seventeen others he was graded lowest in the policy essay; he was appointed gentleman of the palace.
translations.idiomatic: The preface leads into his examination: nominated with Xiahou Zhan and seventeen others, he scored lowest on the policy test yet was made a gentleman of the palace.

sentences.zh: 武帝詔曰：「省諸賢良答策，雖所言殊塗，皆明于王義，有益政道。

translations.literal: An edict of Emperor Wu said, "Reviewing the various worthies’ policy answers, although their words took different paths, all were clear on the king’s righteousness and beneficial to governance."
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wu observed that every candidate’s policy essay, though different, clarified royal principle and helped government.

sentences.zh: 欲詳覽其對，究觀賢士大夫用心。

translations.literal: He wished to read their answers in detail and thoroughly observe worthy gentlemen’s minds.
translations.idiomatic: He meant to study each answer closely to see how these men thought.

sentences.zh: 」因詔諸賢良方正直言，會東堂策問，曰：「頃日食正陽，水旱為災，將何所修，以變大眚？

translations.literal: Thereupon he issued an edict summoning all men recommended as worthy, upright, and plainspoken, convening them in the Eastern Hall for a policy examination, and he said, "Recently the sun was eclipsed at the noon hour, and flood and drought have become disasters; by what means ought we to cultivate our conduct in order to transform this great calamity?"
translations.idiomatic: He then summoned every candidate honored as worthy, upright, and outspoken, brought them together in the Eastern Hall for a policy debate, and asked: "A solar eclipse has lately struck at high noon, and floods and droughts afflict the realm. What must we set right in ourselves and in government to turn aside this grave reproof from Heaven?"

sentences.zh: 及法令有不宜於今，為公私所患苦者，皆何事？

translations.literal: Further, in the case of statutes and ordinances that are not suitable for the present age and that have become sources of suffering to both the public interest and private households—what are all these matters?
translations.idiomatic: Which laws and regulations no longer fit the times, and which policies now torment the state and the people alike? Name them plainly.

sentences.zh: 凡平世在於得才，得才者亦借耳目以聽察。

translations.literal: Generally, peace in the age lies in obtaining talent, and the one who obtains talent likewise borrows ears and eyes in order to listen and inspect.
translations.idiomatic: In any well-ordered age, the decisive thing is to secure the right men; and the ruler who would secure them must lend his ears and eyes wide to what is heard and seen below.

sentences.zh: 若有文武器能有益於時務而未見申敘者，各舉其人。

translations.literal: If there are men possessed of civil and martial abilities who could benefit the pressing affairs of the times yet have not been advanced or had their merits set forth, let each recommend such persons.
translations.idiomatic: If you know men of civil or military gifts who could serve the needs of the hour but have never been brought forward or given a fair hearing, each of you should name them now.

sentences.zh: 及有負俗謗議，宜先洗濯者，亦各言之。

translations.literal: And in the case of those who bear vulgar scandal and slander, who ought first to be cleansed and cleared, let each likewise speak of them.
translations.idiomatic: If there are men smeared by rumor and held in public contempt who deserve to be cleared and restored, speak for them as well.

sentences.zh: 」虞對曰：「臣聞古之聖明，原始以要終，體本以正末。

translations.literal: Yu replied, "I have heard that among the sagely and illumined of antiquity, they traced beginnings in order to grasp endings, and they embodied the root in order to rectify the branch tips.
translations.idiomatic: Yu answered: "The sage-kings of old read the beginning in the end and took their stand on the root so that every twig might grow straight."

sentences.zh: 故憂法度之不當，而不憂人物之失所；

translations.literal: Therefore they worried that standards and measures were not appropriate, and did not first worry that men and things had lost their proper stations;
translations.idiomatic: They fretted first whether the laws were sound, not whether the wrong faces sat in the wrong chairs;

sentences.zh: 憂人物之失所，而不憂災害之流行。

translations.literal: they worried that men and things had lost their proper stations, and did not worry that calamities and disasters were spreading.
translations.idiomatic: they worried whether the right men held the right posts, not whether flood or drought had already broken loose.

sentences.zh: 誠以法得於此，則物理於彼；

translations.literal: Truly, when the laws are obtained aright in this respect, then the pattern of things is ordered in that;
translations.idiomatic: For when institutions are set right here, the natural order of affairs falls into line there;

sentences.zh: 人和於下，則災消於上。

translations.literal: when harmony obtains among those below, then disasters are dispelled among those above.
translations.idiomatic: when those below live in concord, Heaven’s omens of wrath melt away above.

sentences.zh: 其有日月之眚，水旱之災，則反聽內視，求其所由，遠觀諸物，近驗諸身。

translations.literal: If there are flaws in the sun and moon, or disasters of flood and drought, then [the ruler] turns his listening inward, looks within himself, seeks the reason from whence it comes, gazes far at the myriad things, and verifies near within his own person.
translations.idiomatic: Should eclipses darken the luminaries or the seasons bring flood and drought, the wise ruler bends his ear inward, searches his own heart for the cause, scans the world at large, and tests every suspicion against his own conduct.

sentences.zh: 耳目聽察，豈或有蔽其聰明者乎？

translations.literal: For ears and eyes, listening and inspecting—could there be anything that veils their clarity and brightness?
translations.idiomatic: Might something be muffling what he hears or dimming what he sees?

sentences.zh: 動心出令，豈或有傾其常正者乎？

translations.literal: In moving the heart and issuing orders—could there be anything that topples their constant correctness?
translations.idiomatic: Might his passions or his edicts be tilting him off the steady middle course?

sentences.zh: 大官大職，豈或有授非其人者乎？

translations.literal: For great offices and great functions—could there be cases of investing the unworthy?
translations.idiomatic: Have high posts gone to men unfit to bear them?

sentences.zh: 賞罰黜陟，豈或有不得其所者乎？

translations.literal: In rewards, punishments, demotions, and promotions—could there be cases where they do not obtain their proper places?
translations.idiomatic: Do rewards lift the deserving, and do punishments fall on the guilty, or has justice wandered from its mark?

sentences.zh: 河濱山岩，豈或有懷道釣築而未感於夢兆者乎？

translations.literal: By riverbanks and mountain cliffs—could there be those who embrace the Way, fishing between the rocks or building in the wilds, yet who have not stirred dream-portents in the ruler?
translations.idiomatic: Along rivers and among crags, are there hermits of true talent, like the old worthies who fished the Wei or built in the wilderness, still waiting for the dream that calls a king to seek them?

sentences.zh: 方外遐裔，豈或有命世傑出而未蒙膏澤者乎？

translations.literal: Beyond the borders, in distant margins—could there be men whose allotted span commands the age, outstanding heroes, yet who have not received the moistening bounty?
translations.idiomatic: Beyond the pale, in the farthest marches, are there born leaders of the age who have never tasted the court’s favoring rain?

sentences.zh: 推此類也，以求其故，詢事考言，以盡其實，則天人之情可得而見，咎征之至可得而救也。

translations.literal: Extrapolate by categories of this kind, seek their reasons, inquire into deeds and examine words, in order to exhaust the reality—then the circumstances of Heaven and man can be discerned, and when fault-signs arrive, they can be remedied.
translations.idiomatic: Push the inquiry along such lines, trace each ill to its source, weigh deeds against words until the truth stands bare, and the bond between Heaven and humanity will disclose itself; even grave portents may then be turned aside.

sentences.zh: 若推之於物則無忤，求之於身則無尤，萬物理順，內外咸宜，祝史正辭，言不負誠，而日月錯行，夭癘不戒，此則陰陽之事，非吉凶所在也。

translations.literal: If, when pushed against things, there is no opposition, and when sought in the self there is no fault; when the principles of the myriad things are ordered and inner and outer are all fitting; when the invocator’s phrases are correct and words do not betray sincerity—yet the sun and moon run off course and pestilence gives no warning—then this is a matter of yin and yang, not where auspiciousness and inauspiciousness reside.
translations.idiomatic: If nothing in the realm resists your rule, nothing in your breast accuses you, the world runs true within and without, and your prayers to the spirits are honest—yet the lights of heaven still wander and plague stalks the people—then you are watching the turning of cosmic breath, not the ledger of moral fortune and ruin.

sentences.zh: 期運度數，自然之分，固非人事所能供禦，其亦振廩散滯，貶食省用而已矣。

translations.literal: The ordained numbers of timely fate are divisions of the natural order; inherently they are not what human affairs can fully control—one can only shake out the granaries to relieve blockage, reduce food, and curtail expenditures, and that is all.
translations.idiomatic: The span allotted by fate and the reckoning of seasons belong to nature’s own arithmetic; no government can purchase immunity. At most a ruler may open the public granaries, ease hoarded distress, tighten his table, and shave the budget—that is the whole of it.

sentences.zh: 是故誠遇期運，則雖陶唐、殷湯有所不變；

translations.literal: Therefore, if one truly encounters such ordained time, then even Yaotang [Yao of Tao] and Yin Tang would have things they could not change;
translations.idiomatic: When Heaven truly fixes a season of trial, not even the perfection of Yao or the virtue of Tang could have altered its course;

sentences.zh: 苟非期運，則宋、衛之君，諸侯之相，猶能有感。

translations.literal: if it is not ordained time, then the lords of Song and Wei, and ministers of the feudal lords, still could produce a response.
translations.idiomatic: when the times are not locked in such a doom, even middling rulers like those of Song and Wei, or ordinary feudal ministers, could move Heaven by their conduct.

sentences.zh: 唯陛下審其所由，以盡其理，則天下幸甚。

translations.literal: May Your Majesty scrutinize whence these things come, in order to exhaust their principle—then all under Heaven will be greatly blessed.
translations.idiomatic: If Your Majesty will trace each sign to its root and think its logic through to the end, the empire will be the richer for it.

sentences.zh: 臣生長蓽門，不逮異物，雖有賢才，所未接識，不敢瞽言妄舉，無以疇答聖問。

translations.literal: Your subject was raised at a brushwood gate and does not reach to extraordinary things; though there may be worthy talents, I have not met and known them—I dare not speak blindly or recommend rashly, and have no means to array a reply to the sagely questions.
translations.idiomatic: I sprang from a poor lane and never moved in circles where genius shows itself; however many able men the realm may hold, I have not shaken their hands or heard their names. I would not play the blind man naming colors, nor hazard empty nominations, and so I cannot line up answers worthy of your questions.

sentences.zh: 」擢為太子舍人，除聞喜令。

translations.literal: He was promoted to be Gentleman Attendant to the Heir Apparent and appointed Magistrate of Wenxi.
translations.idiomatic: The court raised him to gentleman attendant at the heir’s palace and gave him the magistracy of Wenxi.

sentences.zh: 時天子留心政道，又吳寇新平，天下乂安，上《太康頌》以美晉德。

translations.literal: At that time the Son of Heaven was attentive to the path of government, and moreover the banditry of Wu had just been pacified and all under Heaven was orderly and at peace, so [Yu] presented the "Song of Great Prosperity" in order to praise the virtue of Jin.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor had fixed his mind on good government, and with Wu’s rebels newly crushed the realm lay quiet; Yu therefore offered his "Ode to Grand Concord" to hymn the Jin house’s achievement.

sentences.zh: 其辭曰：

translations.literal: The text says:
translations.idiomatic: It runs thus:

sentences.zh: :於休上古，人之資始。

translations.literal: Oh, splendid high antiquity, the people’s relied-upon beginning.
translations.idiomatic: O glorious dawn of time, cradle of the human race.

sentences.zh: 四隩咸宅，萬國同軌。

translations.literal: The four borderlands all have homesteads; the myriad states share one track.
translations.idiomatic: The four quarters found their homes; ten thousand kingdoms rolled on one wheel-rut.

sentences.zh: 有漢不競，喪亂靡紀。

translations.literal: Han lost its vigor; ruin and chaos knew no measure.
translations.idiomatic: The House of Han faltered, and anarchy knew no end.

sentences.zh: 畿服外叛，侯衛內圮。

translations.literal: The inner domain and outer zones rebelled without; the feudal guard collapsed within.
translations.idiomatic: The heartland’s vassals turned coat beyond the walls, while the royal shield-bearers crumbled within.

sentences.zh: 天難既降，時惟鞠凶。

translations.literal: Heaven’s hardship having descended, the season was only dire woe.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven’s scourge had fallen, and the hour was nothing but grief.

sentences.zh: 龍戰獸爭，分裂遐邦。

translations.literal: Dragons fought and beasts strove, sundering distant domains.
translations.idiomatic: Warriors clashed like dragons and beasts, ripping the far provinces apart.

sentences.zh: 備僭岷蜀，度逆海東。

translations.literal: Liu Bei usurped the title in Min-Shu; Gongsun Du rebelled east of the sea.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Bei seized a throne among the Shu mountains; Gongsun Du defied the throne from beyond the eastern sea.

sentences.zh: 權乃緣間，割據三江。

translations.literal: Quan [Sun Quan] then seized the interval and carved out control of the three rivers.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Quan caught the opening and walled himself inside the land of the three streams.

sentences.zh: 明明上帝，臨下有赫。

translations.literal: Bright, bright High God looks down with blazing majesty.
translations.idiomatic: High God shines terrible and bright above us all.

sentences.zh: 乃宣皇威，致天之辟。

translations.literal: Then He spread the imperial awe and brought down Heaven’s punishments.
translations.idiomatic: He unfurled the emperor’s terror and let Heaven’s axe fall.

sentences.zh: 奮武遼隧，罪人斯獲。

translations.literal: He roused martial prowess east of the Liao passes, and the guilty man was then taken.
translations.idiomatic: Arms thundered beyond the Liao gorges until the rebel chief was caged.

sentences.zh: 撫定朝鮮，奄征韓、貊。

translations.literal: He pacified Joseon and in one sweep campaigned against Han and Mo.
translations.idiomatic: Korea bowed; in a single thrust he swept the Han and Mo tribes.

sentences.zh: 文既應期，席捲梁、益。

translations.literal: The Count of Wen having answered the times, rolled up Liang and Yi like a mat.
translations.idiomatic: When Prince Wen seized his moment, Liang and Shu furled like a scroll before him.

sentences.zh: 元憝委命，九夷重譯。

translations.literal: The arch-evildoer surrendered his fate; the nine Yi submitted double-translated tribute.
translations.idiomatic: The last monster yielded his life; barbarians of nine kinds sent envoys through relayed tongues.

sentences.zh: 邛、冉、哀牢，是焉底績。

translations.literal: Qiong, Ran, and Ailao—there he laid down his achievements.
translations.idiomatic: From Qiong and Ran to Ailao, his merit was carved into those hills.

sentences.zh: 我皇之登，二國既平。

translations.literal: When Our Emperor ascended, the two states were already pacified.
translations.idiomatic: By the day Our Emperor took the throne, the twin rebel realms had already fallen.

sentences.zh: 靡適不懷，以育群生。

translations.literal: There was none far or near who did not cherish him, through whom the multitude were nurtured.
translations.idiomatic: None near, none far, but turned to him with love, and the myriad lives flourished in his shade.

sentences.zh: 吳乃負固，放命南冥。

translations.literal: Wu then relied on its terrain, defying commands in the southern dark.
translations.idiomatic: Wu hugged its rivers and hills and flung defiance into the southern night.

sentences.zh: 聲教未暨，弗及王靈。

translations.literal: Sound and transforming influence had not reached there; the kingly numen did not extend.
translations.idiomatic: Civilizing word had not crossed those waters; the royal aura stopped short of their shore.

sentences.zh: 皇震其威，赫如雷霆。

translations.literal: The emperor shook forth his awesomeness, blazing like thunder.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor uncoiled his majesty, a blaze like spring thunder.

sentences.zh: 截彼江、沔，荊、舒以清。

translations.literal: He cut off that realm along the Jiang and Mian; Jing and Shu were thereby cleared.
translations.idiomatic: He sheared the land between the Long River and the Han; Jing and Yang ran clear again.

sentences.zh: 邈矣聖皇，參乾兩離。

translations.literal: Far-shining sage emperor, pairing with Qian, twinned with Li.
translations.idiomatic: O distant-shining sage, you mirror Heaven’s vigor and ride the fire of insight.

sentences.zh: 陶化以正，取亂以奇。

translations.literal: He moulds transformation with rectitude; he takes chaos with the unexpected.
translations.idiomatic: You shape the age with steadfast right, yet snatch victory from disorder with a strategist’s surprise.

sentences.zh: 耀武六旬，輿徒不疲。

translations.literal: He displayed martial prowess for sixty days; chariots and followers knew no weariness.
translations.idiomatic: For sixty days the drums never cooled, yet neither chariot nor foot soldier flagged.

sentences.zh: 飲至數實，幹旄無虧。

translations.literal: He drank to the return and counted the booty; pennants and yak-tails were undiminished.
translations.idiomatic: The victory cup went round, the tallies matched the spoil, and not one banner-fringe was lost.

sentences.zh: 洋洋四海，率禮和樂。

translations.literal: Vast are the four seas; all tread the rites in harmony and joy.
translations.idiomatic: The four seas roll wide and calm; every shore keeps time to rite and song.

sentences.zh: 穆穆宮廟，歌雍詠鑠。

translations.literal: Solemn the palace shrines; they sing "Yong" and chant "Shuo".
translations.idiomatic: The ancestral temples stand deep in quiet splendor; choirs lift the old hymns of praise.

sentences.zh: 光天之下，莫匪帝略。

translations.literal: Under the illumined heavens, none are not within the emperor’s strategy.
translations.idiomatic: Where sunlight falls, no inch of earth lies outside the emperor’s design.

sentences.zh: 窮發反景，承正受朔。

translations.literal: Where hair grows in the uttermost cold and where shadows bend back, they receive the orthodox calendar and accept the first month.
translations.idiomatic: From the pole where frost never thaws to the tropics where noon casts no shade, all peoples take their calendar from your capital.

sentences.zh: 龍馬騤騤，風于華陽。

translations.literal: Dragon-horses stride proudly; winds blow at Huayang.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven’s steeds prance in proud pairs; auspicious winds gather over Huayang.

sentences.zh: 弓矢橐服，干戈戢藏。

translations.literal: Bows and arrows in cases and quivers; shields and spears are stored away.
translations.idiomatic: Bows sleep in lacquered cases; shields and spears are racked for peace.

sentences.zh: 嚴嚴南金，業業餘皇。

translations.literal: Stately southern metal; towering Yu-huang hulls.
translations.idiomatic: Bronze from the south gleams like a wall; great war-barges ride the waves in ordered pride.

sentences.zh: 雄劍班朝，造舟為梁。

translations.literal: Heroic swords arrayed at court; boats were made into bridges.
translations.idiomatic: Swords of honor fill the hall; hulls are chained into floating bridges.

sentences.zh: 聖明有造，實代天工。

translations.literal: The sage and illumined has a founding deed—truly he substitutes for Heaven’s work.
translations.idiomatic: The holy founder’s handiwork is nothing less than Heaven’s own labor done in human time.

sentences.zh: 天地不違，黎元時邕。

translations.literal: Heaven and earth are not at odds; the black-headed people are at peace in their season.
translations.idiomatic: Sky and soil breathe in tune, and the common folk rest easy in their day.

sentences.zh: 三務斯協，用底厥庸。

translations.literal: The three tasks are thereby aligned, by which their merit is brought to rest.
translations.idiomatic: The three great burdens of state fall into harmony, and true achievement finds its harbor.

sentences.zh: 既遠其跡，將明其蹤。

translations.literal: Having gone far in his tracks, he will clarify his trail.
translations.idiomatic: His footprints already circle the world; his path will shine clearer still.

sentences.zh: 喬山惟嶽，望帝之封。

translations.literal: Lofty Mount Qiao is the marchmount; there lies the fief of the Gazing Emperor.
translations.idiomatic: Mount Qiao lifts like a marchmount where the exile-king once held his narrow domain.

sentences.zh: 猗歟聖帝，胡不封哉！

translations.literal: Ah, our sage emperor—why do you not mount the Feng and Shan sacrifices!
translations.idiomatic: O sage emperor—when will you climb Tai Shan to seal Heaven’s mandate in the ancient rite?

sentences.zh: 以母憂解職。

translations.literal: He resigned office on account of mourning for his mother.
translations.idiomatic: He stepped down to observe mourning for his mother.

sentences.zh: 久之，召補尚書郎。

translations.literal: After a long while, he was summoned and appointed to fill a vacancy as Gentleman of the Masters of Writing.
translations.idiomatic: When the mourning years had passed, the court called him back to fill a post as secretary in the Ministry of State.

sentences.zh: 將作大匠陳勰掘地得古尺，尚書奏：「今尺長於古尺，宜以古為正。

translations.literal: The Chief of Imperial Works Chen He dug the earth and obtained an ancient foot-rule; the Masters of Writing memorialized, "The present foot is longer than the ancient foot; it is fitting to take the ancient as the standard."
translations.idiomatic: Chen He, chief of imperial works, turned up an old measuring rod in the soil; the ministry reported that the current foot outran the ancient gauge and urged the throne to adopt the older length as law.

sentences.zh: 」潘嶽以為慣用已久，不宜復改。

translations.literal: Pan Yue held that because it had been habitually used for a long time, it ought not be changed again.
translations.idiomatic: Pan Yue argued that long custom had fixed the longer measure and that reopening the question would only breed confusion.

sentences.zh: 虞駁曰：「昔聖人有以見天下之賾而擬其形容，象物制器，以存時用。

translations.literal: Yu objected, saying, "Of old the sages discerned the profundities of all under Heaven and sketched their shapes and forms; they imitated things and fashioned implements in order to preserve timely use."
translations.idiomatic: Yu rejoined: "The sages read the hidden pattern of the world and gave it body in tools; they modeled things in bronze and wood so that daily life could keep faith with the seasons."

sentences.zh: 故參天兩地，以正算數之紀；

translations.literal: Therefore they paired three with heaven and two with earth, in order to rectify the reckoning of calculation and number;
translations.idiomatic: They hung the triad on heaven and the dyad on earth to true the abacus of fate;

sentences.zh: 依律計分，以定長短之度。

translations.literal: they relied on the pitch-pipes to compute fen, in order to fix the measure of long and short.
translations.idiomatic: they tuned lengths against the standard pipes so that every inch answered to cosmic pitch.

sentences.zh: 其作之也有則，故用之也有征。

translations.literal: When they made them there was a model, therefore when using them there was verification.
translations.idiomatic: Creation followed a pattern, so use could always be tested against fact.

sentences.zh: 考步兩儀，則天地無所隱其情；

translations.literal: If one examines and paces the two luminaries, then Heaven and Earth cannot hide their conditions from view;
translations.idiomatic: Track sun and moon with honest instruments, and sky and soil cannot cloak their temper from you;

sentences.zh: 准正三辰，則懸象無所容其謬；

translations.literal: if one levels and rectifies the three chronograms, then suspended phenomena can harbor no error;
translations.idiomatic: square the three celestial markers, and the wheel of stars cannot lie about a single night;

sentences.zh: 施之金石，則音韻和諧；

translations.literal: apply them to metal and stone, then tonal resonance is harmonious;
translations.idiomatic: strike them on bell and stone, and every note rings true;

sentences.zh: 措之規矩，則器用合宜。

translations.literal: set them to compass and square, then vessels and tools fit their purposes.
translations.idiomatic: lay them to rule and level, and every vessel sits square to its task.

sentences.zh: 一本不差而萬物皆正，及其差也，事皆反是。

translations.literal: With one root not deviating, the myriad things are all correct; when there is deviation, matters all reverse this.
translations.idiomatic: One true pivot sets the world straight; let that pivot wobble, and everything leans the wrong way.

sentences.zh: 今尺長於古尺幾於半寸，樂府用之，律呂不合；

translations.literal: The present foot is longer than the ancient by nearly half a cun; if the Music Bureau uses it, the pitch-pipes will not accord;
translations.idiomatic: Today’s yardstick overshoots the old by almost half an inch; the musicians’ pipes therefore wander off key;

sentences.zh: 史官用之，曆象失占；

translations.literal: if the historiographers use it, calendrical patterns miss their prognostications;
translations.idiomatic: the astronomers’ almanacs miss conjunction after conjunction;

sentences.zh: 醫署用之，孔穴乖錯。

translations.literal: if the medical offices use it, acupoints go awry.
translations.idiomatic: the physicians’ charts set needles at the wrong depth.

sentences.zh: 此三者，度量之所由生，得失之所取征，皆絓閡而不得通，故宜改今而從古也。

translations.literal: These three are where measures and dimensions arise, and the signs by which gain and loss are taken—they are all snagged and blocked and cannot function; therefore it is right to change the present and follow the ancient.
translations.idiomatic: Music, stars, and healing are the three roots of measure itself, the very gauges of success and failure; with the rod bent, all three choke. The throne should cast aside the modern slip and return to the ancient true line.

sentences.zh: 唐、虞之制，同律度量衡，仲尼之訓，謹權審度。

translations.literal: In the regulations of Tang and Yu, pitch-pipes, lengths, volumes, and weights were unified; in the instructions of Zhongni, the balance should be scrupulous and lengths carefully examined.
translations.idiomatic: The kings of Tang and Yu made pitch, length, volume, and weight sing one tune; Confucius taught rulers to weigh every ounce and measure every span with care.

sentences.zh: 今兩尺並用，不可謂之同；

translations.literal: Now if two foot-rules are used together, one cannot call that "unified";
translations.idiomatic: To run two different feet at once is anything but unity;

sentences.zh: 知失而行，不可謂之謹。

translations.literal: to know error yet proceed, one cannot call that "scrupulous."
translations.idiomatic: to see the fault and march on anyway is the opposite of scruple.

sentences.zh: 不同不謹，是謂謬法，非所以軌物垂則，示人之極。

translations.literal: Not unified, not scrupulous—this is called erroneous law; it is no means by which to regulate things and hand down models, or to show people the ultimate standard.
translations.idiomatic: Neither one nor careful, such rule is simply false measure; it cannot bind the world or hand down an example fit to be the people’s polestar.

sentences.zh: 凡物有多而易改，亦有少而難變，亦有改而致煩，有變而之簡。

translations.literal: Among things generally, some are many yet easy to change, some few yet hard to change; some changes bring vexation, some alterations lead toward simplicity.
translations.idiomatic: Some evils are widespread yet easy to cure, some rare yet stubborn; some reforms breed tangle, others cut straight to clarity.

sentences.zh: 度量是人所常用，而長短非人所戀惜，是多而易改者也。

translations.literal: Measures and dimensions are what people constantly use, yet long and short are not what people cling to fondly—this is a case of "many yet easy to change."
translations.idiomatic: Weights and measures touch every household, yet no one cherishes a wrong inch for sentiment’s sake—exactly the sort of error that can be fixed overnight.

sentences.zh: 正失於得，反邪于正，一時之變，永世無二，是變而之簡者也。

translations.literal: To correct loss by gain, to turn wrong into right, a single moment’s change leaves no second for all generations—this is alteration leading toward simplicity.
translations.idiomatic: Turning mistake into truth in a single stroke leaves no lingering double standard for later ages—that is reform that simplifies rather than complicates.

sentences.zh: 憲章成式，不失舊物，季末苟合之制，異端雜亂之用，當以時厘改，貞夫一者也。

translations.literal: To take the written statutes and established patterns, not losing the old records, and for end-of-season makeshift systems and miscellaneous uses of heterodox oddities, timely to rectify and amend—this is to hold fast to the single true rule.
translations.idiomatic: Honor the written code and the tested pattern, shed nothing the ancestors handed down, and prune away every patchwork fix and stray custom as the seasons demand—that is how a state keeps one faithful line.

sentences.zh: 臣以為宜如所奏。

translations.literal: Your subject holds it right to follow the memorial as submitted.
translations.idiomatic: I believe the throne should accept the ministry’s recommendation.

sentences.zh: 」又表論封禪，見《禮志》。

translations.literal: He also presented a memorial discoursing on the Feng and Shan sacrifices; see the "Treatise on Rites."
translations.idiomatic: He also drafted a long memorial on the Mount Tai rites of sacrifice; the text is preserved in the "Treatise on Ritual."

sentences.zh: 虞以漢末喪亂，譜傳多亡失，雖其子孫不能言其先祖，撰《族姓昭穆》十卷，上疏進之，以為足以備物致用，廣多聞之益。

translations.literal: Because in the turmoil at the end of Han many genealogies were lost, so that even descendants could not speak of their forebears, Yu compiled the "Clarification of Clan Seniority" in ten fascicles and presented it in a memorial, holding that it was sufficient to equip practical use and broaden the benefit of wide learning.
translations.idiomatic: When the Han collapsed, lineage books burned and even sons forgot their fathers’ names; Yu therefore compiled ten scrolls sorting clan precedence and sent them up, arguing that such a record would serve the state’s needs and widen every scholar’s horizon.

sentences.zh: 以定品違法，為司徒所劾，詔原之。

translations.literal: Because in determining rank-grades he violated the law, he was impeached by the Minister of Education; an edict pardoned him.
translations.idiomatic: The minister of education impeached him for bending the rules on official grading, but an imperial rescript let the charge drop.

sentences.zh: 時太廟初建，詔普增位一等。

translations.literal: At the time the Grand Ancestral Temple was first established, an edict universally raised office-rank by one degree.
translations.idiomatic: When the new imperial temple was dedicated, the court ordered every official’s rank raised one step across the board.

sentences.zh: 後以主者承詔失旨，改除之。

translations.literal: Later, because the responsible official had misunderstood the purport of the edict in implementing it, [the measure] was altered and removed.
translations.idiomatic: Later the clerks botched the wording of the decree, and the promotion was rolled back.

sentences.zh: 虞上表曰：「臣聞昔之聖明，不愛千乘之國而惜桐葉之信，所以重至尊之命而達于萬國之誠也。

translations.literal: Yu presented a memorial, saying, "I have heard that among the sagely and illumined of old, they did not spare a state of a thousand chariots yet prized the paulownia-leaf pledge—thereby they honored commands from the supreme seat and conveyed sincerity to the myriad states."
translations.idiomatic: Yu wrote: "The sage-kings of old would not squander a thousand chariots, yet they guarded a boy’s promise scratched on a leaf, for they knew that the word of the throne must weigh more than territory if the empire is to trust its sovereign."

sentences.zh: 前《乙巳赦書》，遠稱先帝遺惠餘澤，普增位一等，以酬四海欣戴之心。

translations.literal: The prior "Edict of the Yisi day" broadly cited the late emperor’s remaining grace and lingering bounty, universally raising office-rank by one degree, in order to repay the joyful allegiance of the four seas.
translations.idiomatic: The earlier amnesty of the Yisi cycle invoked the late emperor’s unfinished kindness and raised every rank one notch to thank the realm for its glad loyalty.

sentences.zh: 驛書班下，被於遠近，莫不鳥騰魚躍，喜蒙德澤。

translations.literal: Dispatch-riders spread the document; it reached far and near, and none did not leap like birds and fish in joy, rejoicing to receive the moistening bounty.
translations.idiomatic: Courier copies flew to every corner, and men bubbled like fish in a spring pool, elated at the sovereign’s shower of grace.

sentences.zh: 今一旦更以主者思文不審，收既往之詔，奪已澍之施，臣之愚心竊以為不可。

translations.literal: Now on a sudden, moreover because those in charge were inattentive in drafting the text, they would withdraw an edict already issued and seize a benefaction already poured out; your servant's foolish heart privately deems this unacceptable.
translations.idiomatic: If, overnight, careless wording by those in charge is now taken as grounds to rescind a promulgated edict and claw back a grant already made, I humbly submit that cannot be justified.

sentences.zh: 」詔從之。

translations.literal: An edict followed it.
translations.idiomatic: The throne approved the proposal by edict.

sentences.zh: 元康中，遷吳王友。

translations.literal: Within the Yuankang years, he was transferred to be Friend of the Prince of Wu.
translations.idiomatic: During the Yuankang era he was appointed Companion to the Prince of Wu.

sentences.zh: 時荀顗撰《新禮》，使虞討論得失而後施行。

translations.literal: At the time Xun Yi was compiling the New Rites; he caused Yu to discuss what was right and wrong, and afterward put it into practice.
translations.idiomatic: While Xun Yi was drafting the New Rites, he had Yu review its strengths and flaws before implementation.

sentences.zh: 元皇后崩，杜預奏：「諒暗之制，乃自上古，是以高宗無服喪之文，而唯文稱不言。

translations.literal: When Empress Yuan died, Du Yu memorialized: "The liang'an regulations come from high antiquity; therefore Gaozong has no wording about wearing mourning, and the text only says he 'did not speak.'
translations.idiomatic: On the death of Empress Yuan, Du Yu argued: "The liang'an observance reaches back to remote antiquity, which is why the inscription for Gaozong says nothing about donning mourning—only that he kept silence."

sentences.zh: 漢文限三十六日。

translations.literal: Han Wendi limited it to thirty-six days.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wen of Han fixed the period at thirty-six days.

sentences.zh: 魏氏以降，既虞為節。

translations.literal: From the Wei house downward, they took the ji sacrifice as the regulating node.
translations.idiomatic: From the Wei dynasty on, the ji sacrifice marked the ritual cutoff.

sentences.zh: 皇太子與國為體，理宜釋服，卒哭便除。

translations.literal: The heir apparent with the state forms one body; by principle it is fitting to release the garments; at the end of wailing immediately remove them.
translations.idiomatic: The crown prince is one with the body politic; he should leave off mourning and lay aside his garb as soon as the final wailing ends.

sentences.zh: 」虞答預書曰：「唐稱遏密，殷雲諒暗，各舉事以為名，非既葬有殊降。

translations.literal: Yu answered Du Yu in a letter, saying: "Tang called it 'stemming music,' Yin called it 'credence in dimness'—each raised an affair to make a name; it was not that after burial there was a special reduction in mourning."
translations.idiomatic: Yu wrote back to Du Yu: "The Tang spoke of silencing music, the Yin of 'credence in dimness'—each named a practice; neither implies a different rule depending on whether burial was already past."

sentences.zh: 周室以來，謂之喪服。

translations.literal: From the Zhou house onward, they called it mourning garments.
translations.idiomatic: Since Zhou times it has been termed mourning dress.

sentences.zh: 喪服者，以服表喪。

translations.literal: Mourning garments: by garments they displayed mourning.
translations.idiomatic: Mourning dress is meant to make bereavement visible.

sentences.zh: 今帝者一日萬機，太子監撫之重，以宜奪禮，葬訖除服，變制通理，垂典將來，何必附之于古，使老儒致爭哉！

translations.literal: Now the one who is emperor in one day has ten thousand offices; the weight of the heir apparent's supervision and nurturing—with regard to it, it is fitting to truncate the rites; when burial is finished remove the garments; changing the system penetrates principle; hand down the norm for the future—why must one attach it to antiquity and make old Confucians wrangle!
translations.idiomatic: The Son of Heaven faces a myriad decisions each day, and the crown prince bears a heavy supervisory charge; it is right to shorten the mourning cycle and end it at burial—adjusting the rules accords with reason and sets a precedent for later ages. Why bind the matter to archaic precedent and set aged classicists at odds?

sentences.zh: 」皇太孫尚薨，有司奏「御服齊衰期」。

translations.literal: When the imperial great-grandson Shang died, the responsible offices memorialized 'imperial garments: zi-cui for one year.'
translations.idiomatic: On the death of Imperial Great-grandson Shang, the authorities requested that the emperor observe one year of zi-cui mourning.

sentences.zh: 詔令博士議。

translations.literal: An edict ordered the erudites to deliberate.
translations.idiomatic: An edict directed the academicians to debate the issue.

sentences.zh: 虞曰：「太子生，舉以成人之禮，則殤理除矣。

translations.literal: Yu said: "When the heir apparent was born, he was raised with the rites of an adult; then the principle of 'early death' is removed."
translations.idiomatic: Yu said: "The heir apparent was welcomed with ceremonies due a grown successor, so the category of a child's untimely death no longer applies."

sentences.zh: 太孫亦體君傳重，由位成而服全，非以年也。

translations.literal: The imperial grandson likewise embodies the ruler and transmits the weight; because of the completion of status the garments are complete, not because of years.
translations.idiomatic: The imperial grandson likewise stands for the sovereign and shoulders the succession; mourning follows from his station, not from his age.

sentences.zh: 」從之。

translations.literal: They followed him.
translations.idiomatic: The court adopted his opinion.

sentences.zh: 虞又議玉輅、兩社事，見《輿服志》。

translations.literal: Yu also debated the jade chariot and the matter of the two altars of soil; see the Record of Carriages and Robes.
translations.idiomatic: Yu also argued the cases of the jade state carriage and the twin earth altars; see Carriages and Regalia.

sentences.zh: 後曆秘書監、衛尉卿，從惠帝幸長安。

translations.literal: Afterward he passed through Palace Library Supervisor and Commandant of the Guards, following Emperor Hui in visiting Chang'an.
translations.idiomatic: He later served as Director of the Palace Library and Commandant of the Guards, accompanying Emperor Hui to Chang'an.

sentences.zh: 及東軍來迎，百官奔散，遂流離鄠、杜之間，轉入南山中，糧絕饑甚，拾橡實而食之。

translations.literal: When the eastern army came to welcome them, the hundred officials fled and scattered; thus he drifted in destitution between Hu and Du, turned and entered the southern mountains, provisions cut off, hunger extreme; he gathered acorns and ate them.
translations.idiomatic: When the eastern relief force arrived, officials scattered in panic; he wandered destitute between Hu and Du, fled into the southern hills, starved when food ran out, and subsisted on gathered acorns.

sentences.zh: 後得還洛，曆光祿勳、太常卿。

translations.literal: Afterward he was able to return to Luoyang; he passed through Grand Coachman and Chamberlain for Ceremonials.
translations.idiomatic: He eventually returned to Luoyang and held the posts of Grand Coachman and Minister of Ceremonial.

sentences.zh: 時懷帝親郊。

translations.literal: At the time Emperor Huai personally performed the suburban sacrifice.
translations.idiomatic: At that time Emperor Huai personally offered the suburban sacrifice to Heaven.

sentences.zh: 自元康以來，不親郊祀，禮儀弛廢。

translations.literal: From Yuankang onward, he had not personally performed suburban sacrifices; rites and observances loosened and were abandoned.
translations.idiomatic: Since the Yuankang era the suburban rites had not been performed in person by the sovereign, and the ritual program had lapsed.

sentences.zh: 虞考正舊典，法物粲然。

translations.literal: Yu examined and corrected old canons; ritual implements were bright and clear.
translations.idiomatic: Yu collated the old regulations so that insignia and ritual gear stood in good order.

sentences.zh: 及洛京荒亂，盜竊縱橫，人饑相食。

translations.literal: When Luoyang-the-capital was wild and chaotic, theft ran rampant; people hungry ate one another.
translations.idiomatic: When the capital fell into chaos, banditry ran rife and famine drove people to cannibalism.

sentences.zh: 虞素清貧，遂以餒卒。

translations.literal: Yu by nature was clean and poor; thus because of hunger he died.
translations.idiomatic: Yu had always lived in austere poverty and died of starvation.

sentences.zh: 虞撰《文章志》四卷，注解《三輔決錄》，又撰古文章，類聚區分為三十卷，名曰《流別集》，各為之論，辭理愜當，為世所重。

translations.literal: Yu compiled the Monograph on Literature in four rolls, annotated the Accounts Resolved concerning the Three Aides of the Capital, also compiled ancient literary pieces, gathering by category and dividing into thirty rolls, named them Collection of Genres by Current, for each he wrote a discourse; phrasing and principle were apt and fitting, and the age valued him.
translations.idiomatic: Yu wrote the four-scroll Treatise on Literature, annotated the Capital Region Records, and arranged ancient belles-lettres into thirty scrolls by genre under the title Collected Genres of Writing, appending a critical essay to each—his contemporaries prized the balance of diction and argument.

sentences.zh: 虞善觀玄象，嘗謂友人曰：「今天下方亂，避難之國，其唯涼土乎！

translations.literal: Yu was good at observing the dark celestial images; once he said to a friend: "Now the realm below is about to be chaotic; a state for fleeing calamity—is it not only the Liang region!"
translations.idiomatic: Yu was skilled at reading the stars; he once told a friend, "The empire is sliding into turmoil—for a bolt-hole, surely nothing rivals the northwest."

sentences.zh: 」性愛士人，有表薦者，恆為其辭。

translations.literal: His nature loved gentlemen; for those who had memorial-recommendations, he always composed their wording.
translations.idiomatic: He delighted in promoting scholars and habitually drafted the memorials for those he recommended.

sentences.zh: 東平太叔廣樞機清辯，廣談，虞不能對；

translations.literal: The Grandee of the Eastern March, Taishu Guang, was pivot-pure and clear in disputation; Guang discoursed at length; Yu could not answer;
translations.idiomatic: Taishu Guang of Dongping was quick and eloquent in debate; in extemporaneous argument Yu could not match him—

sentences.zh: 虞筆，廣不能答；

translations.literal: Yu with the brush; Guang could not answer;
translations.idiomatic: but when brushwork was the test, Guang had no reply.

sentences.zh: 更相嗤笑，紛然於世雲。

translations.literal: Mutually they sneered and laughed; it was confused in the world, they say.
translations.idiomatic: They traded jibes to the amusement of their contemporaries, or so the story goes.

sentences.zh: 束晳

translations.literal: Shu Xi
translations.idiomatic: Shu Xi

sentences.zh: 束晳，字廣微，陽平元城人，漢太子太傅疏廣之後也。

translations.literal: Shu Xi, courtesy Guangwei, a man of Yuancheng in Yangping, was a descendant of Han Heir Apparent Grand Tutor Shu Guang.
translations.idiomatic: Shu Xi, style Guangwei, a native of Yuancheng in Yangping commandery, traced his line to Shu Guang, Grand Tutor to the Han heir apparent.

sentences.zh: 王莽末，廣曾孫孟達避難，自東海徙居沙鹿山南，因去疏之足，遂改姓焉。

translations.literal: At the end of Wang Mang, Guang's great-grandson Mengda fled disaster, from Donghai moved dwelling south of Mount Shalu, thereby removing the 'foot' of Shu, thus changed surname.
translations.idiomatic: Near the close of Wang Mang's reign, Guang's great-grandson Mengda fled the turmoil, moving from the eastern seaboard to the south of Mount Shalu and dropping the lower component of the character Shu, whence the family surname changed.

sentences.zh: 祖混，隴西太守。

translations.literal: Grandfather Hun, Administrator of Longxi.
translations.idiomatic: His grandfather Hun had been Administrator of Longxi.

sentences.zh: 父龕，馮翊太守，並有名譽。

translations.literal: Father Kan, Administrator of Fengyi; both had reputation.
translations.idiomatic: His father Kan was Administrator of Fengyi; both men enjoyed repute.

sentences.zh: 晳博學多聞，與兄璆俱知名。

translations.literal: Xi learned broadly and heard much; together with elder brother Qiu both were known by name.
translations.idiomatic: Shu Xi was erudite and widely read; he and his elder brother Qiu were celebrated alike.

sentences.zh: 少游國學，或問博士曹志曰：「當今好學者誰乎？

translations.literal: In youth he roamed the national school; someone asked Erudite Cao Zhi, saying: "Who today are the fond-of-learning ones?"
translations.idiomatic: As a youth he studied at the imperial academy. Someone asked Academician Cao Zhi, "Who in our day are the true scholars?"

sentences.zh: 」志曰：「陽平束廣微好學不倦，人莫及也。

translations.literal: Zhi said: "Yangping's Shu Guangwei is fond of learning without weariness; people cannot reach him."
translations.idiomatic: Cao Zhi replied, "Shu Guangwei of Yangping—his love of learning never flags; no one can equal him."

sentences.zh: 」還鄉里，察孝廉，舉茂才，皆不就。

translations.literal: He returned to his village; was inspected Filially Incorrupt; was raised Abundant Talent; all he did not go to.
translations.idiomatic: He went home, was nominated Filial and Incorrupt and Recommended Abundant Talent, but declined every appointment.

sentences.zh: 璆娶石鑒從女，棄之，鑒以為憾，諷州郡公府不得辟，故晳等久不得調。

translations.literal: Qiu took in marriage Shi Jian's niece's daughter, cast her aside; Jian took it as resentment, hinted to provinces, commanderies, and ducal offices not to summon him; therefore Xi and others for a long time could not be transferred.
translations.idiomatic: Qiu married a niece of Shi Jian, then cast her off; Jian nursed a grudge and quietly blocked provincial and capital offices from employing the brothers, so Xi and Qiu went years without posts.

sentences.zh: 太康中，郡界大旱，晳為邑人請雨，三日而雨注，眾謂晳誠感，為作歌曰：「束先生，通神明，請天三日甘雨零。

translations.literal: In Taikang, within the commandery border great drought; Xi for the townsmen prayed for rain; in three days rain poured; the crowd said Xi's sincerity moved them; they made a song saying: "Mr. Shu, penetrates spirits and gods; prayed to Heaven three days, sweet rain falls."
translations.idiomatic: During Taikang a severe drought struck the commandery; Xi led the townspeople in a rain prayer, and after three days a soaking rain fell. The people credited his sincerity and sang, "Master Shu moves the spirits—three days of prayer, and sweet rain descends from heaven."

sentences.zh: 我黍以育，我稷以生。

translations.literal: Our millet thereby is nurtured; our glutinous thereby is born.
translations.idiomatic: Our crops revive; our grain springs up again.

sentences.zh: 何以疇之？

translations.literal: How thereby repay him?
translations.idiomatic: How shall we repay him?

sentences.zh: 報束長生。

translations.literal: Repay Shu Changsheng.
translations.idiomatic: Give thanks to Long-lived Shu.

sentences.zh: 」晳與衛恆厚善，聞恆遇禍，自本郡赴喪。

translations.literal: Xi with Wei Heng were thick and good; hearing Heng met disaster, from his native commandery he went to the mourning.
translations.idiomatic: Xi was close to Wei Heng; on learning of Heng's violent death he hurried from his home commandery to attend the funeral.

sentences.zh: 嘗為《勸農》及《餅》諸賦，文頗鄙俗，時人薄之。

translations.literal: Once he composed the Exhorting Agriculture and Cake various rhapsodies; the text was rather vulgar; people of the time despised them.
translations.idiomatic: He once wrote rhapsodies such as Exhorting Farming and On Cakes; the pieces were coarse in style and drew condescension from contemporaries.

sentences.zh: 而性沈退，不慕榮利，作《玄居釋》以擬《客難》，其辭曰：

translations.literal: But his nature was submerged and retiring; he did not admire glory and profit; he made Explaining the Abstruse Dwelling to pattern after The Guest's Reproach; its phrases say:
translations.idiomatic: By temperament he was retiring and indifferent to rank and gain; he composed The Rationale of Secluded Living in imitation of The Guest's Objections, which begins:

sentences.zh: 束晳閒居，門人並侍。

translations.literal: Shu Xi dwelt in leisure; disciples together attended.
translations.idiomatic: Shu Xi lived at leisure, his disciples in attendance.

sentences.zh: 方下帷深譚，隱-{几}-而咍，含毫散藻，考撰同異，在側者進而問之曰：「蓋聞道尚變通，達者無窮。

translations.literal: Just then lowering the curtain deep in talk, leaning on the armrest and laughing, holding a brush scattering pattern, examining and composing similarities and differences; one beside advanced and asked him, saying: "We have heard the Way esteems change and penetration; the perspicacious have no limit.
translations.idiomatic: He had lowered his curtain for a searching discussion, leaned on the low table with a chuckle, poised his brush and scattered fine phrases as he weighed rival views. A disciple stepped forward: "We are told the Way prizes adaptability, and the wise see no final limit.

sentences.zh: 世亂則救其紛，時泰則扶其隆。

translations.literal: Age chaotic then they save its tangle; times peaceful then they support its height.
translations.idiomatic: In troubled times they untie the knot of chaos; in peace they help sustain a flourishing age.

sentences.zh: 振天維以贊百務，熙帝載而鼓皇風。

translations.literal: They raise heaven's net to assist the hundred affairs; they brighten the Emperor's burden and beat the imperial wind.
translations.idiomatic: They shore up the pillars of state and further every task of government, brighten the Son of Heaven's enterprise, and fan the imperial virtue abroad.

sentences.zh: 生則率土樂其存，死則宇內哀其終。

translations.literal: Living, then the whole territory joys in his existence; dead, then the realm within grieves his end.
translations.idiomatic: In life the land rejoices in them; in death the world mourns their passing.

sentences.zh: 是以君子屈己伸道，不恥幹時。

translations.literal: Therefore the gentleman bends himself and stretches the Way; is not ashamed to stem the times.
translations.idiomatic: Hence the noble man bows his person to exalt the Way and does not scorn to meet the needs of the hour.

sentences.zh: 上國有不索何獲之言，《周易》著躍以求進之辭。

translations.literal: Supreme states have the saying 'without seeking how obtain'; the Changes shows leaping to seek advance's wording.
translations.idiomatic: The great polities say, 'Seek not, gain not,' and the Book of Changes urges 'leaping' as the path to advancement.

sentences.zh: 莘老負金鉉以陳烹割之說，齊客當康衢而詠《白水》之詩。

translations.literal: The old man of Shen bore the metal crossbar to set forth cutting-and-cooking discourse; a Qi guest faced the great crossroad and sang the White Water poem.
translations.idiomatic: The elder of Shen shouldered ritual vessels to expound the butcher's art, while a visitor to Qi chanted White Water in the open street.

sentences.zh: 今先生耽道修藝，嶷然山峙，潛朗通微，洽覽深識，夜兼忘寐之勤，晝騁鑽玄之思，曠年累稔，不墮其志。

translations.literal: Now you, sir, drown in the Way and cultivate arts, stand tall like a mountain, hidden brightness penetrates the subtle, harmoniously peruse deep knowledge, night joins forgetting-sleep's toil, day gallops boring-into-mystery's thought, empty years pile up years, you do not fall from your aim.
